about.title: From physics to data
about.paragraphOne: I study Business Intelligence Software Development at ITS ICT Piemonte in Turin, after a university path in physics. That's where my way of approaching a problem comes from: understand the data before writing code, isolate the variables, measure instead of assume.
about.paragraphTwo: I work across the whole chain that turns data into a decision — ingestion and transformation pipelines, databases designed around the questions they have to answer, APIs and interfaces that make the result readable. Python, Java, SQL and Docker are the tools I reach for most.
about.paragraphThree: I'm looking for an internship or a first role in business intelligence and data engineering: real data, real constraints, and people better than me to learn from.

about.subtitle: Business Intelligence Software Developer
about.leadOne: I believe the value of data isn't in how much of it you have, but in whether you can turn it into a decision. That's why I build software that brings together business intelligence, full stack development and artificial intelligence — with real attention to architecture, code quality and the experience of using it.
about.leadTwo: My path started with physics, where I built an analytical and rigorous approach to solving problems. Today I study Business Intelligence Software Development at ITS ICT Piemonte, applying that same method to designing modern, data-driven software.
about.sceneAlt: A badge with Imad El Mir's name hanging from a lanyard: you can drag it with the mouse and it swings.

physics.title: Physics
physics.body: Université Sidi Mohammed Ben Abdellah, Fès: classical and modern physics, calculus, lab work. Two exams short of the degree, and I intend to sit them. What I carry isn't the title — it's the habit of distrusting the first explanation that seems to work. Change one variable at a time, measure, and accept it when the number contradicts the hypothesis. Facing a bug, I do exactly that.

data.title: Moving into software
data.body: The jump was shorter than it looks. Dirty experimental data and a dirty table have the same problem: before you compute anything, you need to know where the values came from and which ones you can trust. From there I got to Python, Java and SQL, then to containers and pipelines, and finally to interfaces — because an analysis nobody can read hasn't finished its job yet.

next.title: Where I want to go
next.body: I'm looking for an internship or a first role in business intelligence and data engineering. I haven't worked in a development team yet, and that's precisely the part I want: real data, real constraints, code review from someone better than me. In the meantime I keep building, because it's the only way I know to find out what I haven't understood yet.

about.bringDescription: Before code I did two other jobs. They're not buried at the bottom of my CV: they taught me three things that matter in technical work more than people admit.

audience.title: Reading an audience's numbers
audience.body: I run social accounts with over 350,000 followers. Every post produces metrics, and the difference between growing and stalling is deciding from those instead of from what you personally like. It's the same question you ask a BI dashboard: what is this number telling me, and what do I do about it tomorrow.

clients.title: Explaining technical things to non-specialists
clients.body: Almost five years as a personal trainer. A training programme only works if the person understands why they're doing it — otherwise they drop it in a fortnight. Turning something technical into something understandable without dumbing it down is a skill, and it can be trained.

discipline.title: Finishing what I start
discipline.body: Six years of MMA and two regional wins, five years in the same gym, an audience built from zero. They all answer the question that actually matters on a first portfolio: does this person see things through? The projects here are the same answer in a different form.

experience.description: Education, work and certifications. Not all of it is computing, and the part that isn't still taught me something I use every day.

its.title: Business Intelligence Software Developer
its.description: An EQF level 5 ITS programme focused on data analysis and software development. It's the course I'm attending now, and where the projects in this portfolio come from.

physics.title: University studies in Physics
physics.description: Studies in general physics, mathematics and scientific method, close to completion: two exams left before graduating. This is where my way of approaching a problem comes from — isolate the variables, measure, verify before concluding.

highschool.title: Scientific high school diploma
highschool.description: Scientific lyceum, with foundations in mathematics, physics and science.

contentCreator.title: Content creator and digital media designer
contentCreator.description: Running social accounts with a community of more than 350,000 followers: producing and editing video content, editorial planning, reading metrics and building organic growth. I learned to read an audience's numbers and decide from them — which is exactly what I ask of a business intelligence dashboard.

personalTrainer.title: Personal trainer
personalTrainer.description: Almost five years guiding people toward measurable goals, adjusting programmes when the data didn't agree. This is the job that taught me consistency, and how to explain technical things to people outside the field.

nutrition.title: Annual training in nutrition
nutrition.description: A year-long programme in nutrition, metabolism and applied dietetics, with a focus on athletic performance.
